title.en: B' Big-Head, B' Big-Gut and B' Tin-Leg
title.zh: 大頭、大肚與鐵腿三兄弟

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XIII 'B' Big-Head, B' Big-Gut, an' B' Tin-Leg'

summary.en: Three orphan brothers with four doughboys each get a fatal excuse: too big a head to climb for water, too big a gut — so Tin-leg climbs, sees Big-gut brushing flies off his doughboy, thinks him eating, kicks and flings himself to death on the coconut tree; Big-gut laughs so much he bursts; Big-head, left alone, fights the eagle for the well-water and is shaken all to pieces.
summary.zh: 無爹無娘的三兄弟，各攜四個麵糰出外取水：頭大者自稱一低頭便倒、肚大者自稱一躬身便跌——只剩鐵腿上樹；他俯見大肚在拂拭麵糰上的蒼蠅，誤以為在偷吃，氣得在椰樹上蹬腿摔死；大肚笑破了肚皮；大頭獨自尋得水井，與搶水的鷹爭執，被鷹搖得粉碎。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian noodlehead-noodlehead tale (numskull cycle). Collected by Edwards from child tellers.

passages.text: This day it was B' Big-head, B' Big-gut, and B' Tin-leg. They had no pa; their ma was dead; they only had four doughboys. So now B' Big-head said, 'Now, brothers, let's go look for water.' They shared out the doughboys, each had a little can, and they went to look for water. They walked till they came to one coconut tree; B' Big-gut said, 'You go, B' Big-head!' B' Big-head said, 'I can't go: if I go, soon as I look down, my head is so big I fall down.' Then he said to B' Big-gut, he go. B' Big-gut said, 'My gut so big if I go I fall down.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, Bahama Songs and Stories, story XIII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now B' Tin-leg said, 'I'll go!' All of them had the doughboys down on the ground. B' Tin-leg was going, climbing up the tree; when B' Tin-leg looked down and saw B' Big-gut brushing the flies off his doughboy, B' Tin-leg thought B' Big-gut was eating it. He just killed himself on the coconut tree, kicking and flinging just so — and B' Big-gut laughed so much till he burst his gut.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then it only left B' Big-head alone. He went to look for water, and came to one well; he was drinking water when B' Heagle came, and the eagle wanted water and B' Big-head would not let him get any. Then him and the eagle had a fight; the eagle kicked him, B' Big-head caught his foot — and after he caught his foot, he couldn't hold it, and the eagle shook him all to pieces. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Rabby Had a Mother: the Fake Funeral

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XIV 'B' Rabby Had a Mother'

summary.en: Hard times: B' Rabby tells his mother to lie on the bed and pretend she is dead, then cries 'Poor B' Rabby got no mother!' to the neighbors — 'go in the room and see for yourself.' When the room is full of mourners come to pay their respects, the boy behind the door with a club locks them in and knocks them down, some killed, some crippled, the balance clear: him and his mother have plenty of meat to eat, though the neighborhood despises them for the dirty trick.
summary.zh: 年歲艱難，兔仔教母親躺床裝死，自己高喊『可憐的兔仔沒了娘！』——『不信自己進屋看去』。待弔客擠滿房間，他持棍反鎖房門痛打：有的被打死、有的殘、其餘逃脫——母子從此有肉有水；只是鄉里因此鄙棄他，他卻答道：『我才不在乎，有肉吃有水喝。』

sensitivity.note: Bahamian Rabby cycle; the fake-death raid is a dark comic tale. Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: B' Rabby had a mother; father was dead; the times were very hard, and they didn't know what to do for a living. B' Rabby said to his mother, 'You lay down on the bed and pretend that you are dead.' So B' Rabby cried out, 'Poor B' Rabby got no mother!' When they asked him where his mother was, he said she was dead — doing that to get food. He said, 'Don't ask me nothing, but go in the room and see for yourself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the neighbors started to go in the room to see the dead mother, B' Rabby stood behind the door with a club in his hands; after the room got full he jumped inside with his club and locked the door, and began to knock down the neighbors — some he killed, some he crippled, and the balance got clear. Him and his mother had a plenty of meat to eat. After that, by him serving such a dirty trick, they despised him and would have nothing more to do with him; and B' Rabby said, 'I didn't care about it; had meat to eat and water to drink.' E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Man, B' Woman and the Monkeys

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XV 'B' Man, B' Woman, an' B' Monkeys'

summary.en: The fake-death raid turned on its planners: the wife lays her poor husband out dead and calls the monkeys to sing — one-tail, two-tail, up to nine-tail, the big nine-tail refusing to enter and standing at the door — and when the 'corpse' rises with a club, he kills everyone but the wary nine-tail and one little three-tail on the roof, who comes down on the woman and sinks her right through the floor.
summary.zh: 假死之計反噬其謀者：婦人將窮夫裝殮，喚來一尾、兩尾以至九尾的猴群唱喪歌；老成的九尾猴不肯進屋，立在門外。『屍』躍起揮棍，殺盡群猴——唯九尾與屋頂上的小三尾倖免；小三尾撲向婦人，把她直沉入地板之下。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian tale; Edwards notes the type's wide distribution. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Now this day it was a poor man who had no money, and wanted to fix a plan to get some. The woman told the man to make believe like he was dead; she dressed the man and laid him out in the house, and when she called all these monkeys she told them to come help her to sing, saying her husband was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: A whole lot of monkeys came — one-tail monkey, two-tail, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine-tail monkey — and the big nine-tail wouldn't come in; he just stood at the door. The woman pitched the song, and when the man got up, so, he killed everyone besides two: the big monkey standing at the door went outside, and one little three-tail monkey stayed up on the roof of the house. When the little three-tail came down on the woman, so, he sank her right through the floor. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XV, middle (1895); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Edwards, story XV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Hopen, Kabendye, Hopen: the Living Cow

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story 'B' Rabby, B' Bouki, an' B' Cow' (the Kabendye formula)

summary.en: Rabby spanks the big cow's flank — 'Hopen, Kabendye, hopen!' — the flank opens, and he fills his pan with meat from the living animal. Bouki begs the secret; Rabby's one warning is do not cut the big thing inside. Bouki cuts the cow's heart, the cow drops dead with him inside, the butchers find a bulging maw and let the 'fresh-beef shopper' out with half the cow as compensation — and when Rabby hears the account he approves the whole market-thriller as the way to do.
summary.zh: 兔仔一拍牛臀念咒『開了，卡本耶，開了』，牛側洞開，他從活牛腹中割滿一鍋肉。布基討得口訣，唯被告誡『莫割腹中大物』；他偏偏割了牛心，牛死己陷；屠者剖出鼓脹的牛胃，放出自稱『來買鮮肉』的布基，賠他半頭牛——兔仔聞罷贊道：『就該這麼辦！』

sensitivity.note: Bahamian tale; Edwards notes its kinship with Vancouver Island and African swallowed-hero tales. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Now this day it was B' Rabby and B' Bouki, and it was blowing; they didn't have nothing to eat and couldn't catch no fish, so they were traveling along to see if they could find something. When B' Rabby looked he saw one big cow; he went to the cow, took his hand, and spanked on the cow's bottom: 'Hopen, Kabendye, hopen!' When the cow's bottom opened B' Rabby jumped in with his knife and his pan and cut his pan full of meat, and said 'Hopen, Kabendye, hopen!' again, and the cow's bottom opened and B' Rabby jumped out — going home with his pan full of meat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, Bahama Songs and Stories, story 'B' Rabby, B' Bouki, an' B' Cow' (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: B' Bouki begged the secret — 'If you don't tell me where you got all that meat I going tell!' — and Rabby gave him the formula with one warning: 'You see one big thing inside there; you mustn't cut that! Mind, if you cut that the cow is going to fall down dead.' Bouki went, spanked the cow's bottom, jumped in, cut his hand full — and, not satisfied, cut the cow's heart: the cow fell down, and Brar' he dead! Bouki cried 'Hopen, Kabendye, hopen!' and, finding the cow's bottom couldn't open, went inside the cow's mouth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning when the people came to feed the cow they found her dead, and began to clean and skin her; they cut her open and took out all her guts — and B' Bouki was inside the maw, swelling up. 'Cut that big thing open and see what's in there!' — and when they cut it open, B' Bouki jumped away yonder: 'See what you threw on me! Ma just sent me down here to buy fresh beef, and you throw all this nasty stuff on me!' The people hushed him and offered half the cow, which he refused — 'I going to carry you to jail!' — and the man threw another stinking pan of water and blood at him, and Bouki jumped yonder again, and the haggling ended with half the cow on Bouki's shoulder. When B' Rabby heard the account he said, 'That's the way to do!' E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: De Man an' de Dog: the Sour-sop Thief
title.zh: 人與狗：偷刺果番荔枝者

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XVII 'De Man an' de Dog'

summary.en: A man keeps a secret sour-sop tree; his wife, suspecting, ties a bag of ashes to his back and so follows the trail to the tree, strips it clean. Denied the last fruit, he offers half to Sheep, Tiger and Lion — each wants all — and Dog takes the bargain for half, then bolts with the fruit with the man after him; the dog buries himself in the sand leaving two eyes out, the man discovers 'the sand has eyes', calls the village to witness the wonder, digs, finds the same dog, and squeezes him dead.
summary.zh: 一人私藏刺果番荔枝樹；其妻疑心，以灰袋縛其背循跡而往，把樹摘個精光。男子以半數誘羊、虎、獅替他取樹梢之果——皆索全部；狗允諾半數，取果而逃，男子窮追；狗藏身沙中只露雙眼，男子驚呼『沙子有眼睛』，召集全村來看奇觀，一掘之下竟是那條狗——將他捏死了事。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian tale. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Now this day it was one man who had one sour-sop tree, and didn't let any people know; his wife and children could hardly get anything to eat, and every morning the man used to go from his house to that tree to eat his breakfast. The woman said, 'I wonder where my husband does get everything to eat.' She got one bag of ashes, and said, 'My husband, come here and let me fix your shirt' — and tied the bag of ashes on his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XVII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the man was going to that tree the ashes dropped out; he went to his sour-sop tree, ate as much as he wanted, and came away. When he came home the woman said, 'My husband, come here; let me fix your shirt again' — and took the bag of ashes off him. After that the woman went there to the sour-sop tree, pulled every one clean, and only left one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XVII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man climbed up in the tree, reached up to that limb with one stick and tried to get his sour-sop down and couldn't. He saw B' Sheep and offered half — 'No, I want all!' B' Tiger wanted all; B' Lion wanted all. Then he saw B' Dog, who agreed to half, caught the fruit — and put off a-running, him and the dog, the man coming on so fast that the dog buried right up in the sand and just left his two eyes out. 'O my! look at the sand got eyes!' The man went and told the people the sand had eyes, and called all the people; when they all came and looked they agreed the sand had eyes for truth — and when the man dug and found out it was that same dog, he caught him and squeezed him dead. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XVII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Devil an' B' Goat, and the Fiddle of Bouki
title.zh: 魔鬼與山羊，及布基的提琴

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XIX 'B' Devil an' B' Goat'

summary.en: The Devil escorts Goat to brother-in-law's dinner with a task-list that destroys him — jump the soft mud while I jump the rock, eat all the sea-grape leaves while I eat the grapes, the cane leaves, the pine-slips, and greet the company as 'Good evening, brutes and 'ogs' — each obedience a disaster and each protest answered 'You fool, you! I didn't tell you to do that!' The next day the same list is offered to Bouki, who echoes every instruction with 'me too' until the fiddle comes out: 'Do you think you going to fool me like you fool B' Goat? You think you going to fool me, but you fool yourself!' — and the Devil kicks him right over.
summary.zh: 魔鬼攜山羊赴妹夫家宴，一路發號施令：跳軟泥、食海葡萄葉、啃蔗葉、嚼松芽，進門還要喊『野獸與豬們，晚上好』——每令皆災，每訴皆被斥為『蠢貨，我可沒叫你那樣做！』次日同一套命令施於布基；布基事事應『我也一樣』，直到提琴響起：『你想像騙山羊那樣騙我？你以為在騙我，其實是騙你自己！』——魔鬼一腳把他踢翻。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian Devil cycle. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: B' Devil asked B' Goat to come down to brother-in-law with him to get some good dinner. Before he got to the brother-in-law there was a place of soft mud, and another place of rock; and B' Devil told him to jump across the soft place and he would jump across the rock. B' Goat stuck in the mud, covered all his eyes — 'Look what you gone caused me to do!' — 'You fool, you! I didn't tell you to jump there!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: They met up with some sea-grape tree, and B' Devil told B' Goat to eat all the leaves while he ate all the grapes — the leaves stuck in his mouth. From the sea-grape tree to the cane field: 'You eat all the leaves and I'll eat all the cane' — and the leaves stuck him in his mouth again. From the cane field to the pine field, the pine-slips stuck him in his mouth; and then, before the house, the greeting: 'Good evening, brutes and 'ogs' — and the brother-in-law kicked him right out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIX, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day he went out with B' Bouki and gave him the same list — jump across the mud, me too; jump across the rock, me too; eat all the leaves, me too; and at the brother-in-law, the same greeting, me too — and everything went smooth, and Bouki got a good dinner. Coming away, B' Bouki got his fiddle and played: 'Do you think you going to fool me like you fool B' Goat? You think you going to fool me, but you fool yourself!' — and B' Devil kicked B' Bouki, and kicked him right over. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XIX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Hellibaby an' B' Dawndejane: the Robbers' Cave
title.zh: 海利寶貝與丹德珍：強盜洞

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XX 'B' Hellibaby an' B' Dawndejane'

summary.en: Two brothers know the cave where the robbers keep plenty money. Dawndejane tests the borrowed tub by touching its bottom, fills his cart with gold — 'Open she-she, open!' — and perishes from greed, torn open and hung on a tree. Three days later his wife sends the brother, who finds him, has a shoemaker stitch him neat — 'I can stitch him neat and sew him neat, but I can put no life in him' — and gains his revenge at the robbers' own dance: oil poured into all the jugs but the head-man's, 'Come in, gentlemens!' — and they kill them all, take charge of the cave, and have been rich from that day till now.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟知曉強盜藏金的洞穴。丹德珍以指探桶底試破借桶之計，念咒『開了，開了』入洞裝車——卻因貪多而不能出，被強盜剖腹吊於樹上。三日後其妻遣弟尋兄，尋得遺體；鞋匠把屍身縫得整齊——『縫是能縫整齊，可我把生命縫不進去』——復在強盜自來的舞會上报仇：除頭目之壺外皆灌沸油，一句『先生們，請進！』，盡誅群盜，奪洞而富，至今。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian Ali Baba-variant (Edwards notes the type). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: There were two brothers, and they knew where the cave was where the robbers kept plenty money. B' Dawndejane sent to buy a tub from the other baby's wife, and to know what he was going to do with the tub she touched the bottom of it. Then he started and went off to the cave; when he got there he said, 'Open she-she, open!' It opened and he went in, filled his cart with money, and afterwards came out and went home — and sent the tub home to the other baby's wife, who raised the tub, looked under it, and found the gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went back to the cave and wanted to bring too much: he filled his cart too full and couldn't get out. The robbers came and caught him, tore him open, and hung him up on the tree. After he didn't come for three days his wife sent his brother to look for him, and he found him in the tree, torn open; took him and put him in a cart and brought him to a shoemaker: 'Can't you stitch him neat? Sew him neat and put life in him?' The shoemaker said, 'I can stitch him neat and sew him neat, but I can put no life in him' — and stitched him neat and sewed him neat, and they buried him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XX, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the robbers came home they missed him, and asked the shoemaker whether he had seen them bring a man dead; they told him yes. They called a dance at B' Dawndejane's house, brought jugs and set them in the jugs — the robbers did. While they were dancing B' Dawndejane told B' Hellibaby's wife to boil two cans of oil and turn it into the jugs — all except one, in which was the head man. When B' Dawndejane went to the door he hollowed, 'Come in, gentlemens!' The head man went in; they killed him, they killed them all — and they went and taken charge of the robbers' cave, and they have been rich from that day till now. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: 'Bout a Bird: the Singing Bird and the Witch Grandmother
title.zh: 說到一隻鳥：會唱的鳥與巫婆祖母

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXI ''Bout a Bird'

summary.en: The witch grandmother starves her orphan grandson on a dare: if he does not find what she hid when he was small, she will kill him. He builds coops — twenty-five, fifty, a hundred — and the witch eats the birds until the hundred-and-first, a very handsome one, is left; it sings 'to-mango' on the housetop and is worth thousands to the sailors. The grandmother sells it for two hundred dollars behind his back, and he burns her in a tar barrel for it.
summary.zh: 巫婆祖母以藏物為難孤兒：找不到幼時她藏起的東西便殺了他。他造雞籠——二十五、五十、一百——巫婆把鳥吃盡，只剩第一百零一隻極俊美的鳥；它在屋頂唱起『去-曼果』之歌，身價數千金。祖母背著他把鳥賣了兩百塊，他便把她燒進了瀝青桶。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian wonder tale. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: The fellow's father and mother were dead, and his grandmother was a witch, what he used to stay with. He hid something — eh, when he was small — and when he grew big she told him that if he didn't find it, she would kill him. He made twenty-five coops; each one of them caught birds and she ate them. He made fifty: 'I know she can't eat them!' She ate them, fifty. He made a hundred: 'I know she can't eat a hundred!' She ate ninety-and-nine of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The one that was left was a very handsome bird. He took it out and fed it, and it went up on the house and began to sing: 'Le, y, o, tu-low to mango; pan-ar, jan-ar, tu-low to mango.' When he looked, he saw an old sailor coming, who asked where all this music was coming from: 'It isn't any music at all; all the music here, little bird's got it.' Asked what he would sell him for — 'Nothing!' — then what would he let him sing for — 'Two thousand!' The sailor gave him his two thousand dollars; another came, and the singing was four thousand — and the sailors paid their thousands and carried the bird aboard the schooner, where it flew from the companion to the gaff, from the gaff to the jib-stay, and from the jib-stay flew back to its old master again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his owner went out to walk, he and his lady; when he came home his bird was gone — the grandmother had sold him for two hundred dollars. He told her if she didn't find it he would burn her in a tar barrel; and the next day the bird came home. Still he burned his grandmother in the tar barrel. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Parakeet an' B' Frog: the Singing Contest for the Bride

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXIII 'B' Parakeet an' B' Frog'

summary.en: Nine acres to cut down in a week for the eldest daughter and three hundred dollars: Mister Frog claims the work with a boast-song that fells not a leaf, while Parakeet, bagged and hidden, does the clearing from the treetop. Each visit of the daughter exposes the fraud a little more — the pretty song she half-heard, the kiss withheld, the shame of Frog sunk under the dry leaves with only his head out — until the girl goes home and tells her father, and Parakeet marries the lady and gets her three hundred dollars.
summary.zh: 一週砍倒九畝地，可得長女與三百金：青蛙先生自誇『天下的勞動者，數我青蛙最勤勞』，唱而不落一葉；被裝袋藏起的鸚鵡卻在樹頂把地清完。姑娘每次到訪都多識破一分——那支更好聽的歌、那個索而未得的吻、羞得青蛙伏在枯葉下只露一顆頭——直到她回家告父；鸚鵡娶得姑娘與三百金。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian wonder tale (impossible-task courtship). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: You know there was a man who had nine acres of ground to cut down, and he said that if he could get anybody to cut it down in a week, he would give him his eldest daughter to wife and three hundred dollars. Mister B' Frog said, 'I think if there's any workingman in the world, Mister B' Frog is the man!' He started, met Mister B' Parakeet, and offered him a good breakfast to come and help cut down the ground; he put him in a bag and carried him, and when he got there Mister B' Frog got up in a tree and sang his boast — 'I think if there's any workingman in the world, Mister B' Frog's the man; Quaw-quaw-waw!' — and not a leaf did drop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXIII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mister B' Parakeet came out and went up in a tree and commenced to sing — and half an acre fell down. When B' Frog saw the man's daughter coming he said, 'Parakeet, come down out of that tree; get in this bag; don't let them see you' — and when she got there she said, 'I think if there's any workingman in the world, Mister B' Frog is the man.' He asked her for a kiss: 'No, wait till tomorrow.' The next day she came back again and asked what pretty song she had heard him singing before she got there — and he asked her for a kiss, and she gave it to him. Mister B' Parakeet didn't like it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXIII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day B' Parakeet went again with B' Frog and got up in a tree and began to sing — and B' Frog begged him for God's sake to come down and get in the bag, but he said, 'No, I ain't coming down today!' The girl came in the field, and B' Frog sunk under the dry leaves and just left his head out, he was so ashamed. She said, 'I thought it wasn't Mister B' Frog doing all this work!' — went home and told her father; and B' Frog wanted to beat Mister B' Parakeet, who cried 'Cut him off in the east!' and Frog turned and ran to the westward — 'Cut him off to the westward!' — until B' Frog met a goat and owned that all that fray between them was done. Mister B' Parakeet married the lady and got her three hundred dollars. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXIII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: A Young Lady an' 'er Son: the Forbidden Drum

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXVI 'A Young Lady an' 'er Son'

summary.en: The lady has a drum in the house and forbids her son to beat it: if he beats it, the spirits will drag him away. Gone out on a hearing, the boy gets the drum and knocks 'Mama gone in bay-road, Papa soon come back, only poor me won't — Dumeracker, Dumeracker, I wan' to go!' — and when he looks, the spirits are coming: 'Boy, beat that thing again; let me dance!' Unable, he bribes B' Monkey with three shillings' flakes of tobacco from his pa's trunk, and the monkey keeps the drum going all day until the spirits go away.
summary.zh: 家中有一面禁鼓：打了它，精靈便會把人拖走。母親外出聽道，男孩取鼓敲起——『媽媽去了灣路，爸爸快要回來，只剩我可憐——杜梅拉克，杜梅拉克，我想去！』——擡眼精靈已至：『小子，再敲！讓我跳！』他敲不動了，從父親的箱子裡取三先令的煙絲雇猴替敲；猴子敲了一整天，精靈方散。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian spirit-drum tale; the 'spirits' of Bahamian tellings are the duppy/jumbey powers. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: The lady had a drum in the house; she told her son not to beat it — that if he would beat it, the spirits would drag him away. After she was gone out on a hearing he got the drum and commenced to knock: 'Mama gone in bay-road, Papa soon come back, only poor me won't — Dumeracker, Dumeracker, Dumeracker, Dumeracker, I wan' to go!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he looked he saw the spirits coming, who said, 'Boy, beat that thing again; let me dance!' He said, 'I can't knock!' — 'O B' Frog, come knock this thing for me!' — 'I can't knock.' — 'O B' Yabby, knock this thing for me!' — 'I can't knock.' — 'O B' Monkey, knock this thing for me!' — and B' Monkey said, 'I tell you what I do: go to your pa's trunk and get me three shillings' flakes of tobacco.' He went and got him the tobacco; B' Monkey put one piece in his mouth and commenced to knock the drum. He kept B' Monkey knocking all day; after that the spirits went away. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVI, ending (1895); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVI, tail (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Goat, B' Bouki, an' B' Rabbit: the Chain and the Pit
title.zh: 山羊、布基與兔仔：金鏈與陷坑

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXVII 'B' Goat, B' Bouki, an' B' Rabbit'

summary.en: An old man steals Rabby's splendid chain, then uses its ransom to ride his donkey-errands — from hill to hill to the house in the valley — leaving the rabbit at each stop 'you ride me a little farther'; the rabbit answers with pebble-soup dinners, one-cord fires and a knock of the fork, then makes off with the man's gold band and horse, lures him into Rabby's own parlor over a trap-door, and buries him to the chorus 'Full up, mah, full up, pa!'
summary.zh: 老頭兒偷走兔仔的金鏈，又以歸還為名叫他馱驢代勞——從這山到那山、再到谷中的屋子——每站都說『再馱我一程』。兔仔以石頭湯、一捆柴的火與敲叉試熟的騙局周旋，最後盜走老頭的金箍與馬，把他誘進自家客廳的活板陷阱，合唱著『填滿啦，媽，填滿啦，爸』把他埋了。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian master-rider trickster tale. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: They went in the sea one day, and B' Rabbit had a very splendid chain around his neck; an old man came and took his chain. 'Oh, B' Bouki and B' Goat; come, go get me my chain.' — 'You want your chain, go yourself; we ain't going with you.' B' Rabbit started and ran till he caught up the old man: 'Master, please to give me my chain.' — 'You ride me from here way to that hill yonder, I give you your chain.' He rode him from there to that hill, set him down, asked again — 'Now ride me from that hill way to that other hill, way yonder, and I give you your chain' (he wanted to kill B' Rabbit) — put him down, asked again — 'Ride me to that house in the valley, way yonder, and I give it to you.' He rode him to that house, and the man took him and threw him in the house: 'You stay there.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man had a gold band and a horse. Coming toward dinner time he asked what the rabbit's mother gave him for his dinner: 'My ma always gives me pebble soup.' The man filled the pot full of pebbles; asked how much wood — 'Three cords' — and got one cord, burnt that out, took his fork to try them to see if they were done, and when he struck them they went Ka-bang! Then he started to go for the other cord — and B' Rabbit went and took the man's gold band and horse, got home and hid the band and horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man started to look for his horse; the first house he came to was B' Rabbit's house. 'Oh, little boy, you see any little boy go by with a horse and drum?' — 'Yes, Masse'; I see him go way up the street.' — 'Old man come get some sour.' B' Rabbit had a hole dug under the floor with some boards laid on it, and set the man's chair right over that hole, and the table. After the man was finished eating, B' Rabbit gave him a pipe to smoke; the fellow laid on the arm-chair and commenced to smoke — and B' Rabbit took his feet and moved away the board: the old man went down, table, chair and all. B' Rabbit sung out, 'Full up, mah, full up, pa!' — and they filled the hole right up and beat it down; and thus ended that old story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman an' 'er Husban': the Doctor's Warm Bath
title.zh: 婦人與丈夫：醫囑的『溫浴』

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXVIII 'The Woman an' 'er Husban'

summary.en: The doctor orders a warm bath for the very sick husband; the literal-minded wife heats the oven as hot as she can, sweeps out the coals, sets him inside and stops the oven up. At her return she finds him sitting up grinning — 'It's doctor's orders: grin and bear it!' — and when next she comes to take him out, 'O God, my husband's dead!' — and the doctor's answer is the tale's own: 'You fool, you! I didn't tell you to do that; I told you to put him in a warm bath.'
summary.zh: 醫生為重病的丈夫開了『溫水浴』；一字不差的妻子把烤爐燒得滾燙、掃出炭火、將丈夫置入、封上爐門。回來探視，見他坐起咧嘴——『這是醫囑：咬牙忍著吧！』——再去看時，丈夫已死，她奔去找醫生；醫生答曰：『你這蠢婦！誰叫你那樣做？我說的是溫水浴！』

sensitivity.note: Bahamian numskull-noodlehead anecdote. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Now a woman whose husband was very sick went to the doctor to see what she must do for him; the doctor told her she must put him in a warm bath. She went home and heated the oven as hot as she could, then swept the coals out and set him inside of her — stopped the oven up. When she went to it through the day to take him out, behold, he was sitting up grinning. She said, 'It's doctor's orders: grin and bear it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVIII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she went to take him out she said, 'O God, my husband's dead!' — and ran off for the doctor, who said to her, 'You fool, you! I didn't tell you to do that; I told you to put him in a warm bath.' E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXVIII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXIX 'B' Big-Head an' B' Little-Head'

summary.en: Pears eaten, water sought: Big-head insists on drinking first, and the more he drinks the more his head grows until it is stuck in the hole of water. Little-head can't pull him out; 'O God, B' Big-head, look at the Devil!' — and when Big-head raised, he broke his head off and left it in the hole, going home running with no head, and that ended the old story.
summary.zh: 吃完梨子去找水：大頭執意先飲，愈飲頭愈大，直到卡進水洞；小頭拉不出來，喊道『天哪，大頭，快看魔鬼！』——大頭一抬，腦袋斷落在洞中，無頭狂奔回家——老故事就此收場。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian noodlehead tale. Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: B' Big-head and B' Little-head went for a walk one day, and met up by a whole lot of pears; they sat down and ate all they wanted. After they were finished eating the pears they went to look for some water, and met up by a hole of water. B' Big-head said to B' Little-head, 'Let me drink first.' B' Little-head said, 'No, let me drink first' — and stooped down and drank as much as he wanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXIX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: B' Big-head went to drink; the more B' Big-head used to drink, the more his head used to grow — and when he had enough he said, 'O B' Little-head, come pull me out!' — 'I can't pull you out!' He caught hold of him and pulled and couldn't pull him out: 'O God, B' Big-head, look at the Devil!' When B' Big-head raised he broke his head off and left it in the hole, and went home running with no head — and that ended the old story. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXIX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: De Girl an' de Fish: Conch-o, Conch-o-wally
title.zh: 姑娘與魚：康喬-康喬瓦莉

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXXI 'De Girl an' de Fish' (the Golden Fish type; Edwards notes Fortier's variant)

summary.en: A girl catches a little fish out of a conch shell, names him Choncho-wally, keeps him in the well and feeds him three meals a day until he is a big fish — summoned by her song 'Conch-o, Conch-o-wally, don't you want to marry me, my daddy short-tail?' Her brother learns the password and their father goes with a fish-spear, sings the song, strikes the fish and serves it for dinner; the girl carries food to the well and sings three times to a silent water, and then cries herself to death behind the house.
summary.zh: 姑娘從螺殼中捉得一尾小魚，命名『康喬瓦莉』，養於井中，一日三餐以歌相喚——『康喬，康喬瓦莉，你可願娶我，我的短尾爸爸？』弟弟偷學口令，父親持魚叉循歌而至，擊斃大魚烹為晚餐。姑娘提食到井邊，唱了三遍，井水無聲——她躲到屋後，哭死了。

sensitivity.note: Golden Fish type (Edwards cites Fortier's variant); collected from child tellers.

passages.text: This day this girl went down to the sea for salt water, and caught one little fish out of a conch shell; she named him Choncho-wally, put him in the well, and every morning she used to put some of her breakfast in the bucket and carry it to the fish, and some of her dinner, and some of her supper — she fed him till he got a big fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: This morning, when she went to carry the breakfast for him, she sang: 'Conch-o, Conch-o-wally, don't you want to marry me, my daddy short-tail?' — and he came up and she fed him, and let him go down. When she went home the boy said, 'Pa, sister got something inside the well.' The next day she came again with vittles, and the man sent the boy behind the tree to listen to what she was going to sing: 'Conch-o, Conch-o-wally, don't you want to marry me, my daddy short-tail?' The boy caught it, went and told his pa, and the man took his grange (fish-spear), went, sang the song — and the fish came up; he struck him, carried him home, and they had some for dinner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the girl took some in the bucket to carry to the fish; when she went to the well to call the fish she sang, 'Conch-o, Conch-o-wally' — she sang again — she didn't hear no fish and she didn't see none — she sang again, and began to cry now. Then she went home to the house, behind the house, and she cried herself to death. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Boys an' One Woman: the Grinder's Razor
title.zh: 三童與老嫗：磨刀的石輪

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXXII 'Three Boys an' One Woman'

summary.en: Three fortune-seeking boys lodge with a rich old woman who eats people. Under the bed they hear her at the grindstone singing 'You turn the grindstone, I sharpen the razor, shark-a-she, shark-a' — and the youngest answers 'O gren-di, gren-di, what make you do so?' — with the excuse that his mother always greets him with the fat of the biggest cow. While she kills the cow he cuts three banana-suckers, lays them under the bedstead, takes her money and goes; the razor falls three times on banana-suckers — the third cuts through the floor and burns down the house, old lady and all.
summary.zh: 三個尋寶的男孩投宿於食人的富嫗家中。床下聽得她在磨石旁唱『你轉磨輪，我磨利剃刀，沙卡-舍，沙卡』——最小的應聲『格倫迪格倫迪，你這是做什麼？』並謊稱母親素以最大母牛之脂相迎。趁她殺牛，男孩截三段香蕉苗置於床下、捲走金錢；滾燙的剃刀三次落下——第三次穿透地板，連屋帶嫗燒了個精光。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian ogre-house tale (Hansel-and-Gretel frame). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Three boys went to look for a fortune one day, and met up by an old woman, very rich, but still she used to eat people. The little boy said, 'Old woman, please to let me sleep here tonight.' She told them, 'All right,' and put them under the bedstead to sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she thought they were asleep she got up and got a razor, and went to the grindstone, singing: 'You turn the grindstone, I sharpen the razor — shark-a-she, shark-a!' Then the youngest boy jumped up and sung: 'O gren-di, gren-di, what make you do so?' — 'Little boy, little boy, why won't you go to sleep?' — 'My ma always kills the biggest cow she got and greets me with the fat.' While she was killing the cow he went and cut three banana-suckers, laid them under the bedstead and sent his other two brothers along; then he went and took her money.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: She went to the grindstone and commenced to sing that same song, and while she was grinding the razor the boy went with the money. When she came in she thought the boys were under the bedstead, and was going to kill them then: she took her razor and cut one banana-sucker in two (she thought that was a boy she was cutting), cut the second banana-sucker in two, cut the third banana-sucker in two — and the razor was so hot it went through the floor and burned down the house, old lady and all. That's the whole story. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: A Lady an' 'er Two Dawtahs: the Cart in the Roof
title.zh: 夫人與二女：屋梁上的馬車

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXXIII 'A Lady an' 'er Two Dawtahs'

summary.en: Two suitors — one in cassimere, one in a diagonal suit with a beaver, who is B' Devil — and the sisters choose by cloth, the younger taking the Devil. Her brothers, paid in rice and pork, haul a coconut-tree pulled up rootless and a whole cart into the sister's roof; when the Devil sits to dinner the rope is cut, cart and tree fall through the floor, the Devil runs away, and the sister is carried home.
summary.zh: 兩位求婚者——一位著細呢、一位著斜紋呢戴海狸帽——後者正是魔鬼；姊妹們以衣料擇婿，妹妹嫁給了魔鬼。她的兄弟們以米飯豬肉受雇，把連根拔起不斷一鬚的椰樹與整輛馬車吊上妹妹家的屋梁；魔鬼甫坐下進餐，繩索一斷，車樹轟然穿落——魔鬼逃走，妹妹被接回家。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian wonder tale (Devil-husband escape). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: Once it was a lady who had two dawtahs. This day two gentlemen went to the house: one had on cassimere, the other had on a suit of diagonal with a beaver — and that was B' Devil. The youngest dawtah said to the eldest, 'Which one you love best out of the two?' — 'I love the one that's got on the cassimere.' The youngest said, 'I love the one that's got on the diagonal best' (she wanted good clo's!). So the two got married: B' Devil took his wife and carried her to his house, and the eldest one married not far from her ma and was living at the east.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXIII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother had two boys, and the youngest asked for two bits to bring his sister home; his mother hushed his nonsense — his sister had been married a year ago. He bought twelve pence of rice and a threepence of pork, cooked it, and his brother came and asked for some: 'I'll do anything you want me to.' So he gave him the rice, harnessed the horse and cart, and the two started. At a coconut tree first: 'Pull up that coconut-tree without breaking a root in it.' — 'I can't, brother!' — 'Give me my rice!' — 'I can't give you your rice, now we eat it!' — and anyhow, he pulled up the coconut-tree without breaking a root in it, put it in the cart, and they went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXIII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: They got to the sister's house, took the horse out of the cart, hoisted up the cart in the roof of the house — and the coconut-tree. She went and called B' Devil out of the field, telling him that her brothers were coming, and had the table all ready to embrace them so they could eat. When B' Devil came he sat to the table; when he was eating the boy stood up and cut the rope away, and the cart and the coconut-tree fell down on the floor. It frightened B' Devil and he runned away, and the boy took his sister and carried her home. That ended the story. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXIII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Jack an' B' Snake: the Half-hitch

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXXIV 'B' Jack an' B' Snake' (Edwards notes Jack-the-Giant-Killer ancestry)

summary.en: The Queen promises Jack untold money if he can kill the snake, and her daughter if he can clear the rice-field of rice-birds. Jack's weapons are insults disguised as flattery: the snake's body, he reports, can't go in this half-hitch — the vain snake comes out to prove it and is drawn taut and cut up by the soldiers; the rice-birds, he reports, can't all fill this basket — and every one of them flies in to disprove it. 'Here the rice-birds,' says Jack; 'you can get married to my daughter,' says the Queen.
summary.zh: 女王懸賞：能誅蛇者賞銀無數，能清盡稻田雀群者可娶公主。傑克的武器是裹著奉承的激將：『他們說你的身子鑽不進這半結套索』——虛榮的蛇出洞自證，被收緊索套、亂刃分屍；『他們說滿籃的雀，你們雀群填不滿』——群雀爭相入籠自證。『雀在此』，傑克道；『可娶吾女』，女王道。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian Jack cycle (European Marchen in 'old story' dress). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: The Queen said, 'B' Jack, if you can kill this snake, I don't know how much money I wouldn't give you!' So Jack said, 'I want five hundred dollars to go on a spree.' So he gone up there now and said, 'B' Snake, what you think these foolish people say? They say your body can't go in this half-hitch.' He come out of the hole and went in the half-hitch; then Jack drew the half-hitch taut, and all these soldiers came around and cut him up in pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXIV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: So then the Queen said, 'Jack, I got one more trial for you to do. If you could go up there in this cornfield and kill all the rice-birds, I let you get married to my daughter.' He went to the field to the rice-birds, and B' Jack said, 'B' Rice-birds, what you no think these foolish people say? They say all of you rice-birds can't fill up this basket!' The rice-birds said, 'Why, people so foolish — no, all us rice-birds can't fill up that basket!' So all the rice-birds went in the basket, and B' Jack drew the basket together with the rice-birds in it, and went home to the Queen: 'Here the rice-birds.' — 'Well, B' Jack, you can get married to my daughter.' E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXIV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (2024 print) (1895), story XXXV 'B' Little-Clod an' B' Big-Clod' (Edwards notes the Bahama version of Andersen's Little Claus and Big Claus)

summary.en: Big-Clod works Little-Clod's horse for nothing and slaps him down for touching his own; Little-Clod sleeps beside his grandfather and swaps the beds, so that Big-Clod cuts off the grandfather's head by mistake for his rival's — and the grandson sends the dead grandfather a glass of beer, fixes on his head, and the beer-carrier who slaps the 'sleeping' head off earns three thousand dollars for a decent burial. Little-Clod digs him up and carries him down to market, and the tale of the horse-skin and the hominy and the tailor in the big chest runs on to the Andersen ending.
summary.zh: 大克拉德白白使喚小克拉德的馬，還因他自家用馬而掌摑放逐。小克拉德睡在祖父身旁、暗中調換鋪位——大克拉德誤把祖父當作情敵砍了頭。孫子竟給亡祖送上一杯啤酒、把頭安回，還託運酒人代送；運酒人以為死者假寐，一掌又把頭拍落——賠償三千金的『體面安葬』就此成交。小克拉德掘屍上市，馬皮、冷粥與大箱裡的裁縫接踵而至——直奔安徒生式的結局。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian Little-Claus variant (Edwards notes the Andersen kinship). Collected from child tellers.

passages.text: B' Little-Clod had one horse and B' Big-Clod had two. B' Big-Clod used to take B' Little-Clod's horse and work him, and give him nothing to eat; B' Little-Clod got vexed and went to take B' Big-Clod's horse to work too — and when he went to take his horse, B' Big-Clod slapped B' Little-Clod down and sent him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Just let me sleep here tonight!' He slept alongside his grandfather, B' Little-Clod did; B' Big-Clod put B' Little-Clod in front and his grandfather over the back — and B' Little-Clod went over the back and put his grandfather in front. And B' Big-Clod came and cut off his grandfather's head, because he thought it was B' Little-Clod. And next morning B' Little-Clod went to buy one bottle of beer, sent his grandfather a glass of it — what was dead — and fixed on his grandfather's head, and still had him laying down; and he sent it with the man which he bought the bottle of beer from. When the man went he said, 'Sir!' and slapped him beside the head to make him wake — he thought him asleep and knocked his head off. Then B' Little-Clod began to cry, and the man said, 'No, don't cry; I'll have him buried decent, and I'll give you three thousand dollars besides, if you don't make no noise.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXV, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He dug him up and carried him down to market, where they were going to put him in jail, saying he had killed one old man. Coming back, dark caught him in the road and he asked a man to let him sleep there that night — in the old horse stable, all right sir. The old man did ask him if he was hungry, and gave him some cold hominy to eat; and when he was done eating he went in the horse stable and sat down, and as he was sitting down the man's wife came past and asked what he wanted there: 'Your husband sent me here to sleep tonight.' When B' Big-Clod did kill his horse he had his horse-skin in his hand and tied it round his feet; the woman did give her husband cold hominy to eat — and all the good things she had for the tailor she put on the shelf, and some in her bed, and put the tailor in a big chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: And then they were sitting down in the house, the three of them — the little boy, the man and his wife — and the man asked the little boy to pitch a riddle, and the boy said, 'I don't feel like pitching no riddle!' — 'You know your mother and your father learned you some riddles' — 'All right, ma. My riddle, my riddle, ma-rendi-ho; perhaps you can tell me this riddle, and perhaps you can't: my mother had a hog had twelve pigs bigger than the twelve horns that was in the oven...'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XXXV, ending (1895); not verbatim.
